newsitem.title: UK: Dollar may stunt developing world oil demand growth.
newsitem.headline: Dollar may stunt developing world oil demand growth.

text.p: The sharp rise in the U.S. dollar could hit oil demand in developing countries, the engine for growth in world consumption, right when the blistering rally in crude prices has cooled off, analysts said on Friday.

But in Europe, higher taxes will insulate consumers because a smaller percentage of the retail price is exposed to fluctuations in the dollar, the currency used to price crude oil on international markets, they said. Falling diesel prices, growing in popularity as an automotive fuel, will also soften the impact of a strong dollar.

"In countries where the excise duty is particularly low, as in developing countries, then yes, they will be affected more by the strengthening dollar than in Europe," one analyst who tracks world oil demand trends said. "If demand in these countries slows down, there will be an impact on global demand growth".

Taxes in India account for about 30 percent of the gasoline price and in Taiwan 45 percent, while in Europe the tariffs grab as much as 80 percent of the pump price, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Indian demand ballooned by 8.8 percent in 1996, versus a 10.6 percent growth rate in 1995, the IEA said.

World oil demand in 1997 is estimated to increase by 1.9 million barrels per day (bpd) or 2.6 percent to 73.7 million bpd. Non-OECD demand is projected to grow by 4.2 percent or 1.3 million bpd to 31.9 million bpd.
"In the long run the changing exchange rate has a long run impact" on demand, said Paul Horsnell, research fellow at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies.
This month the dollar jumped to a 34-month high against the German mark and multi-year peak against the Japanese yen.
In Japan, oil product prices effectively rose 60 percent in 1996 from 1995, in part from the dollar's strength against the yen, according to Salomon Brothers.
"This will put additional downward pressure on demand growth," analysts at Salomon said in a recent report.

"Indeed, one cannot rule out the possibility that with the oil price peak...earlier this year and the dollar strengthening, the producers are worried that the explosive growth in oil prices will suppress demand, both in the short and long term," it said.
The spot Brent Blend crude futures contract on London's International Petroleum Exchange reached a post-Gulf War high of $25.06 a barrel in October and then retested $25 in January.
It tumbled below $20 on Friday, the lowest price for the spot contract since August, but is still about $2.50 above a year ago.
European retail petroleum product prices, already swollen by high taxation, have not risen as sharply in percentage terms as in other parts of the world.
Retail gasoline prices in Germany rose only 6.6 percent in January versus a year ago, but excluding taxes were up 25 percent, according to the IEA.
The French automotive diesel market saw prices up 11.9 percent from a year ago, compared to a 31 percent rise excluding taxes.

"In most parts of the world the rising dollar impact will be cushioned by these higher taxes," said Peter Bogin, associate director at Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris. "I would not use the dollar as a strong factor in determining demand right now."
In fact, because developing countries were more dependent on oil, their demand was less elastic to changes in price and foreign exchange rates, analysts said.
